questions.q: Per this lesson, what determines which integration pattern actually fits a given requirement?
options: Whichever pattern was used on the team's most recent prior project
Honestly answering the four framing questions from Lesson 1 (who initiates, how often, how much data, how fast) and following where the answers lead
Whichever pattern the available developers already know best, regardless of the requirement
Always defaulting to the most recently released Salesforce feature
questions.explain: Pattern choice is meant to be the output of honestly answering the four framing questions for the specific requirement at hand, not a matter of habit, familiarity, or precedent from an unrelated prior project.

questions.q: A requirement involves syncing 500,000 records nightly. According to this lesson's framework, what does that volume answer rule out?
options: It rules out asynchronous patterns entirely
It rules out synchronous, per-record API calls for the batch, pointing instead toward Bulk API or a scheduled batch pattern
It rules out using Salesforce as either the source or the target
It rules out using any middleware or iPaaS layer
questions.explain: High volume specifically rules out synchronous, per-record API calls as impractical at that scale, and points toward a purpose-built large-volume mechanism like Bulk API or a scheduled batch pattern instead.

questions.q: In the worked example, why does Lead conversion triggering a marketing-platform update point toward fire-and-forget rather than a synchronous callout?
options: Because fire-and-forget is always faster regardless of the scenario
Because the triggering transaction (converting the Lead) has no business reason to wait on the marketing platform's response
Because marketing platforms cannot be called synchronously under any circumstances
Because Lead conversion volume is always too high for a synchronous call
questions.explain: The deciding factor is coupling tolerance: the Lead-conversion transaction doesn't need to know the outcome of the marketing-platform update to complete correctly, so there's no business reason to block it waiting on another system's response.

questions.q: What specific risk does this lesson warn about when a pattern decision is made after implementation has already started, rather than during the architecture phase?
options: Sunk-cost bias — a team reluctant to rework already-written code even once its flaws become apparent
Increased hardware costs, which only occur during the architecture phase
Loss of access to the Bulk API if implementation starts too early
Automatic violation of Salesforce's terms of service
questions.explain: Choosing a pattern after code already exists invites sunk-cost bias: the team that's already written a synchronous implementation resists reworking it into an asynchronous design even once volume or coupling problems surface, which is why the decision belongs to the architecture phase, before implementation starts.

questions.q: Which of the four framing questions specifically separates a requirement that genuinely needs an immediate answer from one that only feels urgent but can tolerate a short delay?
options: How much data is involved
Who initiates the integration
How often the integration runs
How fast the integration needs to respond (timing/urgency)
questions.explain: The timing/urgency question is specifically what separates a true immediate-answer need (pointing to synchronous) from a requirement that merely feels urgent but can tolerate asynchronous request-reply or fire-and-forget.
